html:
The Lord of Sipán was a ruler of the Moche people of northern Peru who died around 250 CE, aged about 35 to 45. His tomb, found untouched by looters at Huaca Rajada near Sipán in 1987, was one of the great archaeological finds of the 1900s.

The Moche built large adobe pyramids on the north coast and made some of the finest pottery of the Americas, including portrait vessels of real people. The Lord was buried with gold and silver ornaments, a gold sceptre, necklaces of gold and silver peanuts, and the bodies of attendants, guards and a dog.

The Peruvian archaeologist Walter Alva excavated the tomb after police caught looters nearby. The finds showed that scenes on Moche pots of warriors and priests were real ceremonies. They are in a museum at Lambayeque. Like Machu Picchu, the Lord has become a symbol of the past of Peru.
